title: Is 3% interest a 3% gain?
hook: Your savings pay 3% a year. Prices rise too. What does your balance really buy?

knows: that inflation erodes what cash buys (inflation lesson)
doesNotKnow: how to net interest against inflation
the idea of a real interest rate

misconception: If my account pays 3% I am gaining 3%.
objective: The learner can explain that what money can buy depends on interest relative to price rises (the real rate, roughly interest minus inflation), so 3% interest with 5% inflation leaves you able to buy about 2% less.

claims.text: $100 at 3% interest becomes $103 after a year; a basket costing $100 today costs $105 after a year of 5% inflation.
With 3% interest and 5% inflation, your $103 buys what about $98.10 buys today, about 1.9% less.
The real interest rate is (1 + interest) / (1 + inflation) − 1.
claims.source: Fisher relation; e.g. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, chapter 'Measuring the Cost of Living' (nominal vs real interest rates); chapter numbers vary by edition.

claims.text: For small rates the real rate is roughly interest minus inflation (here 3% − 5% = −2%).
When inflation equals the 3% interest rate, the money buys exactly as much as today; above it, less; below it, more.
claims.source: 1.03/(1 + π) is 1 at π = 0.03, below 1 for π > 0.03 and above 1 for π < 0.03.

claims.text: The lesson is a model with illustrative rates: one year, one basket, no tax.
claims.source: Assumptions of the lesson's own calculation in Demo.tsx.

recall.question: A loan charges 4% a year while prices rise 6%. Roughly what is the real interest rate?
recall.why: The real rate is roughly interest minus inflation: 4% − 6% ≈ −2% (exactly 1.04/1.06 − 1 = −1.9%).
